findings.message: stories/jobs/job-20261020-wake-cycle-astronaut-jun-3923f7/drafts/story.r1.json line 361 says Jun looked at 'the thin gap on the map and the tool pack by the wheel'. The route wake > locker or oru-log > ... > threshold > cut-engines can reach this ending with no dust-map clue, no tool-pack, or neither (every pack and chart choice has a skip option). The ending then names things the reader never found. Reword so it does not depend on items or clues, or split the line by what the reader holds.

Draft line 331: 'The big rock showed on the left.' The clue (line 28) says the lane is left of the rock, and climax-lane (line 263) and ending-1 (line 302) put the rock on the right. The rock side contradicts itself.

Draft lines 201 and 205: Dex says 'I lost my pack in the shake' and offers a spare, but the locker pack (line 53) is tagged as his and may already be in Jun's pack. The same applies to the rack pack at captain-wakes (line 133). A reader who already holds the pack is offered a second one with no acknowledgement. Add a line for the reader who has it, or make the offer depend on not holding it.
Draft line 146 calls the lane 'a thin dark lane'. The dust-map clue (line 28) and climax-lane (line 264) call it clear or glowing white. Use one description.

Choices 'lamp-on' (line 180) and 'tools-on' (line 192) are both labelled 'Smile at Dex'. They are single-option passages with an empty decision. Use a label that tells the reader what happens next, such as 'Ask Dex what is next'.

Locked choice 'use-clicker' (line 276) hint reads 'You need a tool pack with a clicker light.' It does not say where one can be found (the locker, the Captain's rack or Dex's bench). The threshold hint (line 252) is fair. Because the route never returns, only a replay can use the hint, so name the places.

Skills practised: Reading and following this story practises decoding wh, ck and tch words in meaningful context, and recognising the same word-set words again on every route. It builds sequencing (latch, switch, hatch; tools in order), inference (green and amber pod lights, a map that does not match bent sensors), and vocabulary from context (sensors, coolant, navigator). Choices and locked hints ask the reader to track clues and items, so they also practise comprehension monitoring and cause-and-effect reasoning.

Word sets meet their minimums with wide margins (wh 35/10, ck 35/8, tch 30/8) and every listed word is used. Every word carries its declared pattern: when, white, whisper, wheel, whistle, whip (wh); back, deck, click, neck, pack, rock (ck); catch, match, latch, hatch, watch, switch (tch). Each set appears on the shortest route to all five endings (per-ending counts 10 to 23). Most uses read naturally, for example 'A soft click woke Jun Adair' (wake), 'The latch gave a click' (captain-wakes) and 'Dust whispered along the hull' (storm-bridge).

'He gave a whip of his wrist and the clamp snapped tight' is the least natural set-word use. 'Whip' as a noun for a quick flick is unusual for a 10 to 13 reader. A common word such as 'flick' would read more easily, but 'whip' is already used elsewhere in the wh set. Consider whether another wh word fits better here.

'Watch' is a tch word whose vowel is not the short a of 'hatch' or 'match' (it follows the w-a pattern). It is also used as a noun in 'watch crew'. The spelling pattern is correct, but a learner may need support with the vowel sound. 'Whistle' has a silent t and a -le syllable, and 'wheel' and 'white' contain vowel teams or silent e. The brief names no decodability stage, so I could not judge whether these fit the child's current level.

Left and right carry the key clue ('left of the big rock'). Ending 3 says 'The big rock showed on the left' and then 'Now I see the lane'. That sits oddly with the lane being left of the rock (climax-lane puts the rock on the right). Left/right confusion is common for dyslexic readers. Narrative-designer: fix the ending-3 direction and consider a landmark cue, such as the rock's colour or shape, alongside left.

Ending 5 refers to 'the thin gap on the map and the tool pack by the wheel'. The cut-engines choice has no requirements, so a reader who never found the map clue or the pack meets items they do not have. Ending 2 says 'a clicker light and a good map would help', although reaching climax-lane required the map clue. Both lines can confuse a reader's picture of what they hold.

Dex's voice 'crackled from the engine room' in storm-bridge, but captain-wakes says the comm panel is dark and 'Our calls cannot get out'. A reader may not see why Dex can speak to the bridge when no one else could. Say that the ship's inside speaker still works, or that only outside calls fail.

The glossary entry 'anomaly' is never used in passage text. It appears only in the premise metadata, so word help will never show it in the story. Either use the word in a passage, for example when Oru names the dust, or drop the entry. The other eight glossary words are used.

The story is about 1,477 words in total, with an average sentence of 6 words. A route is roughly 500 to 700 words, which is much shorter than the stated 25 minutes. The very short sentences also read young for ages 10 to 13, though the themes (calm under pressure, teamwork, delayed consequences in ending 4) suit that age and no passage is heavy. Consider telling the parent the real reading time, or having the narrative-designer add a little more varied sentence length in a later revision.

I did not run a script for the stricter 16-word limit, so this is a manual check, not a measured one.

story.r3.json lines 98 and 104-106: Oru states the order (latch, switch, hatch) in the text just before the choice, so the sequencing choice has no real thinking in it. The two wrong choices go to not-yet (line 110), which then does the steps for the reader. Not harmful, but it is a weak puzzle.

story.r3.json lines 133-134, 205-206, 220-221 and 150-151: several pairs of choices (take or skip the spare pack, copy the lane or trust memory, study the dust shapes or take the wheel) end at the same passage. shelfSummary.blurb: A space survival mystery: a navigator wakes early on a drifting ship and must wake the crew and steer clear of a dust storm. It practises wh, ck and tch words, plus -ed endings, beginning blends and FLOSS words. Readers also practise sequencing, inference and vocabulary from context.

findings.message: Skills practised: Reading and following this story practises decoding wh, ck and tch words in meaningful context, and meeting the same word-set words again and again on every route. It builds sequencing (latch, then switch, then hatch; tools sorted and passed to Dex in order; climbing to the bridge together step by step), inference (the whistle in the vents that signals the dust is closer, the crew's last call naming the engine room, green and amber pod lights, bent sensors that make maps untrustworthy) and vocabulary from context (sensors, coolant, anomaly, navigator, and now what a latch, switch and hatch each do). The new branches add short detour scenes that ask the reader to notice a detail (a spark near the wire, tools sorted in order) or choose to bring a companion along, so the story also practises comprehension monitoring, cause-and-effect reasoning and reading dialogue for meaning, same as before.

Word sets still meet their minimums with wide margins (wh 38/10, ck 46/8, tch 35/8), every listed word is still used, and no concept mismatches are reported. The six new passages carry set words naturally in context, not as lists: 'A thin whistle moved through the vents' and 'Jun's neck prickled' (locker-listen), 'Good catch,' said Dex' and 'Back up a little' (dex-lamp-watch), 'Click. Click. Each tool found its place' (dex-tools-sort, onomatopoeia for sorting, not a drill), and 'a wall of white' (storm-engine-together). Each set still appears on the shortest route to all five endings (wh 10 to 13, ck 20 to 25, tch 13 to 17), the same spread as revision 3 plus the small addition from the new branches.

'not-yet-why' has Oru explain three tch words in a tight run: 'The latch unlocks... The switch wakes the heartbeat... The hatch lets in air.' Each clause gives the word a distinct job, so it is not a bare list, but it reads closer to a vocabulary drill than the story's usual natural dialogue. This is a genuine comprehension beat (it answers 'why does order matter', which is the point of the detour), so I am not requesting a change, but the narrative-designer may want to loosen the parallel phrasing in a future pass.

Carried over from revision 3, still present and unaddressed because it was out of this revision's scope: 'He gave a whip of his wrist' (dex-tools) is still the least natural use of a set word, 'catch' and 'match' still get only 2 uses each (lopsided practice inside the tch set), and the storm-bridge leak line and the captain-wakes reading-time note from the prior review still apply. None of these affect whether the word-set minimums or every-route coverage pass, so they do not change this verdict.

The six new passages (locker-listen, oru-log-crew, not-yet-why, dex-lamp-watch, dex-tools-sort, storm-engine-together) are all short, read at the same 6-to-10-word average sentence length as the rest of the story, and I found no sentence over the brief's 16-word limit in them by manual count (the longest, in storm-engine-together, is 'At the top, the dust storm filled the window in a wall of white,' 14 words). The analyzer's 20-word threshold also reports none over.

Limits of this review: the analyzer matches spelling, not sound, and only checks the shortest route to each ending, not every possible route through the new branches. It does not judge decodability, vocabulary level or story quality. I read every new and changed passage in revision 4, checked each named choice point for a genuine second decision (not a decoration), and traced the new branches back into the existing graph by hand, but did not play every route in the app. I am an AI agent; this is a pre-review, not the human literacy gate, and does not replace a qualified human literacy reviewer.

findings.message: story.r4.json lines 314-324 versus storm-engine lines 299-312: storm-engine places the backup wheel 'on the wall' in the engine room with no travel implied, but the new bring-dex-along branch has Jun and Dex 'climbed the steps together... At the top, the dust storm filled the window in a wall of white' before reaching the same threshold passage. The two routes to the same next passage imply different geography (wheel in the engine room vs. a climb to a window at the top of some stairs). Not a dead end or soft lock, and a young reader is unlikely to notice, but worth a line tightening the backup wheel's location so both branches agree.

story.r4.json lines 128-130: unchanged from r3 and still a weak puzzle - Oru states the pod order (latch, switch, hatch) right before the three-way choice, so picking switch-first or hatch-first has no real inference behind it. The r4 fix (not-yet / not-yet-why) adds a genuine second choice after a wrong guess, which helps, but the original choice at `bridge` itself still is not a real decision. Carried over from review-3-qa; out of this revision's scope per revision-notes.r4.md, so not blocking.

story.r4.json lines 171-172: unchanged from r3. Carried over from review-3-qa; not touched by this revision.

story.r4.json lines 82-85 versus dex-chart lines 287-290: unchanged from r3. Carried over from review-3-qa; not touched by this revision.

Unchanged from r3: the take-or-skip-spare-item choice pairs still reconverge immediately and only add or skip an inventory item/clue (thin choice design). Narrative-designer's revision notes confirm this was intentionally left out of scope for r4. Not a defect (engine de-duplicates items), just a reminder it is still open.

Skills practised: following Jun through the pod bay, the engine room and the dust storm practises sequencing (the 'latch, switch, hatch' pod-opening order at bridge/not-yet/not-yet-why/captain-wakes; tools sorted and passed to Dex in order at dex-tools/dex-tools-sort), inference (the whistle in the vents that signals the dust is closer at locker-listen; the crew's last call naming the engine room at oru-log-crew; green vs amber pod lights; bent sensors that make maps untrustworthy), vocabulary from context (sensors, coolant, anomaly, navigator, and what a latch, switch and hatch each do), detail (ten-then-twenty pod checks, the tool pack's clicker light paying off at the climax) and comprehension/engagement across the five branching endings. The wh/ck/tch word sets are not decoration: 'pack', 'click'/'clicker' and 'latch'/'switch'/'hatch' are load-bearing plot nouns (the inventory item, the climax tool, the pod puzzle), so decoding practice and story comprehension reinforce each other rather than competing.

Verified the six passages fixed for the single-choice defect in this revision (locker-listen, oru-log-crew, not-yet-why, dex-lamp-watch, dex-tools-sort, storm-engine-together) by reading them directly and diffing r4 against r5: the only changes are the six new choices plus one label tweak ('Open the pod in the right order, step by step'), exactly as the revision notes describe. Each new choice reads naturally and several reinforce target words in context rather than diluting them: 'Skip the talk and lift the latch now' (not-yet-why, reinforces 'latch'), 'Go straight to Dex's wall chart' / 'Head over to Dex's wall chart' (dex-lamp-watch/dex-tools-sort, no target word but no false pattern either), 'Hurry down to the engine room instead' / 'Hurry straight to the engine room' (locker-listen/oru-log-crew), 'Ask Dex to check the sensors once more first' (storm-engine-together). None of the six new choices introduce a word that merely looks like a target pattern without carrying it (no 'who'/'ache' style false friends).

literacy.r5.json's automated checks all read ok (word-set minimums wh 38/10, ck 46/8, tch 36/8; every listed word used; no concept mismatches; each set on the shortest route to all five endings; target concepts present; 0 sentences over the analyzer's 20-word cutoff). I cross-checked this by hand: the per-ending-route counts in literacy.r5.json are byte-identical to literacy.r4.json (wh 10-13, ck 20-25, tch 13-17 across the five endings), confirming the six new r5 choices did not shorten any route or remove a target word from any path to an ending — the fix added real alternatives without touching word-set coverage. I also manually counted every sentence in the draft (not just the analyzer's 20-word threshold): the longest sentence in the whole story is 15 words ('Next time, Jun thought, a clear plan and the right tools would help even more.', ending-2), inside the brief's 16-word limit, including in the newly-touched passages.

Two tch set words are thinly used: 'catch' and 'match' appear only twice each (vs. 7-9 for hatch/watch/switch/latch), unchanged from earlier revisions. The set total (36) clears the minimum (8) with room, so this does not block, but a future pass could give 'catch' or 'match' one more natural use to even out the practice. Also unchanged: 'He gave a whip of his wrist' (dex-tools) is still the single least natural use of a set word in the story (a literary idiom rather than a concrete action), though it is not incorrect.

Limits of this review: the analyzer in literacy.r5.json detects spelling patterns, not sound — it would, for example, treat any 'wh' word the same regardless of how a child actually pronounces it, and it does not judge decodability, vocabulary level or story quality on its own. Its route check only follows the shortest path to each ending, not every possible path through the graph (I separately traced the specific new-r5 bypass routes, e.g. wake→locker→locker-listen→engine, by hand to confirm word-set words still appear). I read every passage and choice in story.r5.json myself, including all six passages changed in this revision, and compared r4 and r5 directly; I did not play the story in the app. I am an AI agent and this is a pre-review: it is not the human literacy review the publication policy requires, and a qualified human reviewer must still confirm these linguistic claims before the story can be marked passed.

findings.message: story.r5.json lines 158-172: the two choices added by this revision both target `captain-wakes` and neither carries an `effects` block (contrast with the item/clue-gated reconvergences at captain-wakes/dex-fixed/dex-chart/storm-bridge, which do add or withhold tool-pack/dust-map). Picking 'Open the pod in the right order, step by step' (line 169) or 'Skip the talk and lift the latch now' (line 170) produces byte-for-byte the same next passage, same state, same remaining path. This is not a genuine branch point, it is the exact defect this revision set out to remove (a passage with only one real way forward), now wearing two buttons instead of one, and it fails MASTER_SPEC.md line 48 ('Passages connected through meaningful choices'). Revision-notes.r5.md's claim that this matches 'the take the item or don't pattern already used and passed by QA elsewhere' does not hold up: those four passages differ by an item/clue gain, this one does not differ at all.

story.r5.json lines 328-342: same defect as not-yet-why. 'Face the storm together' (line 339) and 'Ask Dex to check the sensors once more first' (line 340) both target `threshold` with no effects on either branch, and `threshold` (lines 344-365) never acknowledges that a sensor re-check happened. The promised action in the new choice's label has no narrative or mechanical payoff; whichever button is pressed, the reader gets the identical next passage. Same product-spec and revision-notes concerns as the not-yet-why finding above.

story.r5.json lines 238-252 (dex-lamp-watch, choice `go-to-chart` line 250) and 268-282 (dex-tools-sort, choice `go-to-chart-tools` line 280) both skip straight to `dex-chart`, bypassing `dex-fixed` (lines 283-297). `dex-fixed` is the only remaining place an engine-route reader can pick up the `tool-pack` item (`take-bench-pack`, line 294) if they never visited `locker` or `captain-wakes`. I traced this concrete, reachable route: wake -> ask-log -> ask-oru-more (oru-log-crew) -> hurry-to-engine-crew -> engine -> pass-tools -> sort-tools -> go-to-chart-tools -> dex-chart -> storm-engine -> ... -> threshold -> thin-lane (unlocked via dust-map from oru-log) -> climax-lane -> use-clicker, which is now LOCKED because tool-pack was never offered. Compare this to every other place the story lets a reader go without the pack (captain-wakes `skip-rack-pack` line 187, dex-fixed `skip-bench-pack` line 295): each of those is an explicit, informed decline ('no pack needed' / 'Thank Dex, no pack needed'). The new dex-lamp-watch/dex-tools-sort shortcuts silently remove the only remaining pack offer with no indication in the choice label that doing so forfeits the item, and this was not possible in r4 (dex-fixed was mandatory on every engine-room route per the r4 draft I diffed). This is a regression introduced by this revision's fix, not a pre-existing condition, and it quietly makes the clicker-triumph ending (ending-1) unreachable for a valid, player-discoverable route without ever telling the reader they gave something up.
